# Evidence: copy frameworks

Ratings:

- **measured**: a study or a large dataset with a stated method (peer reviewed, or with its data shown).
- **survey**: a stated sample, self-reported.
- **practice**: experienced practitioners' documented method or observation; nobody measured it.
- **vendor**: a seller's own data about what it sells.
- **untraced**: repeated widely, no source found, or the source does not say it.

"(summary)" after a source means only an abstract, a record or a retelling was read. Every URL is in `sources.md`.

|---|---|---|

## Origins

| Claim | Source | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| E. St. Elmo Lewis devised AIDA in 1898 | Strong 1925, repeated everywhere | untraced (disputed) |
| No evidence shows Lewis created a prototype around 1898; Sheldon and Dukesmith made the decisive contributions | Iwamoto 2024 (summary) | measured (historical research, peer reviewed) |
| The 1898 formula appeared anonymously in Printers' Ink, 9 Feb 1898 | Wikipedia, citing the issue | practice (secondary, cited) |
| The acronym AIDA was first used by C. P. Russell, Printers' Ink, 2 June 1921 | Wikipedia, citing the issue | practice (secondary, cited) |
| Sheldon added Satisfaction in *Successful Selling* (1911) | Wikipedia | practice (secondary, cited) |
| Dukesmith used attention, interest, desire, conviction in 1904 (the AIDCA steps) | Wikipedia, citing *Salesmanship* 2(1) | practice (secondary, cited) |
| AIDCA as a named formula has an author | none found | untraced |
| ACCA comes from Colley's DAGMAR report to the ANA, 1961, a goal-setting model | Wikipedia and summaries | practice (secondary) |
| PAS has an identified inventor | none found | untraced |
| Schwartz (1966) prescribes name the need, dramatize it, present the product as the inevitable solution, for prospects with a need they do not connect to a product | *Breakthrough Advertising*, ch. 2, read | practice (primary text) |
| Dan Kennedy called PAS "the most reliable sales formula ever invented" in *The Ultimate Sales Letter* (first ed. 1990) | Secondary quotes; catalog record for the date | practice (wording not checked) |
| PASO's Outcome step was added by Belinda Weaver, 2019 | Her post, read | practice |
| PASTOR's six steps are Problem, Amplify, Story and Solution, Transformation and Testimony, Offer, Response, by Ray Edwards | His own post, read | practice (primary text) |
| BAB has an identified inventor | none found | untraced |
| FAB was invented at Xerox in the 1950s | Circulates; nothing confirms it | untraced |
| In large sales, features and advantages draw more objections; only benefits tied to a need the buyer stated go with success; advantages beat features in small sales | Rackham, *SPIN Selling* 1988, Huthwaite's 35,000-call study (summary) | measured (observational, proprietary, never independently replicated; read through summaries) |
| The "So what?" test has a known coiner | none found | untraced |
| The 4Ps were invented by Henry Hoke in the 1930s | One cut-off reading note of a Spitz book | untraced |
| Bob Bly's *Copywriter's Handbook* teaches Picture, Promise, Prove, Push | Reader's highlight (summary) | practice (unverified) |
| The 4 U's were devised by Michael Masterson and Bill Bonner, for bullets | AWAI 2001, read | practice (primary, publisher is their own company) |
| QUEST was created by Michel Fortin in the late 1990s at Algonquin College and expanded in *The Death of the Salesletter* (2006) | Fortin's own page, read | practice (self-reported) |
| Fortin: in B2B the Qualify stage is almost always underinvested | same | practice |
| SLAP has an identified author | none found | untraced |
| Star-Story-Solution was created by Vince James and adapted by Brunson | One Substack post | untraced (single source) |
| Hook-Story-Offer is Brunson's, in *DotCom Secrets* (2015), *Expert Secrets*, *Traffic Secrets* (2020) | Publisher page, podcast summaries | practice |
| Brunson: an underperforming funnel is always the hook, the story or the offer | Podcast summary | vendor (his own businesses) |
| The 1-2-3-4 formula has a named author | Copyblogger article, no author | untraced |
| Monroe's motivated sequence dates from Alan Monroe at Purdue, mid 1930s | Course texts (summary) | practice (secondary) |

## Schwartz, Caples, Ogilvy

| Claim | Source | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| Schwartz describes five states of awareness under his own headings (Most Aware; Knows of the Product But Doesn't Yet Want It; new products for a known want; products that solve needs; Completely Unaware) | *Breakthrough Advertising*, ch. 2, read | practice (primary text) |
| A headline that works at one stage of awareness fails at another; the stages are separated by "a psychological wall" | same | practice |
| For an unaware market: no price, product, function or desire in the headline; an identification headline whose only job is to get the next paragraph read | same | practice |
| Five stages of sophistication: claim, enlarged claim, mechanism, enlarged mechanism, identification | *Breakthrough Advertising*, ch. 3, read | practice |
| In the fifth stage of sophistication the market no longer believes advertising and only identification with the prospect works | same | practice |
| Schwartz's stages rest on published test data | None in the book's chapters read | untraced |
| A used car dealer's general headlines flopped; specific cars with make, year and price brought three times as many customers who "answered the ads", "by actual count" (newspaper ads, not a keyed split test) | Caples, *Tested Advertising Methods* 1997, read | practice (counts reported as a story) |
| "97,482 people" is stronger than "nearly 100,000" because it sounds like a count | Caples 1997, read | practice |
| Most copy stays general because specific data takes time and trouble to collect | Caples 1997, read | practice |
| "Specifics are more believable than generalities"; "What you say is more important than how you say it"; headlines that "appeal to the reader's self-interest or give news" work best | Ogilvy, foreword to Caples' fourth edition, read | practice (primary text) |
| Caples' rules come from keyed-coupon tests of real ads | Caples 1997 and Ogilvy's foreword, read | practice (method stated, data mostly not shown) |
| "The more informative your advertising, the more persuasive it will be" is Ogilvy's | Quote collections; book not read | practice (attribution not checked) |
| Ogilvy took the Rolls-Royce clock line from a technical editor's report | Secondary write-ups | practice (secondary) |
| A Pierce-Arrow ad used a similar line decades earlier | One secondary source | untraced |

## Applied to LinkedIn (this pass's inferences)

| Claim | Basis | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| Most cold LinkedIn readers are at Schwartz's stage 4 or 5 | They do not know the sender; many do not name the problem (also `../personas/`) | practice (inference) |
| Most B2B services sold by cold message face a fifth-stage sophistication market | Schwartz's definition applied to the volume of similar outreach; agrees with the personalization data in `../linkedin-messages/` | practice (inference) |
| Spend PAS's words on efficacy and proof, not agitation | O'Keefe and Hoeken rows above; agitation complaints in `../cold-email/` (survey) | measured (ingredients), practice (application) |
| "Urgent" (4Us) and Brunson-style urgency are risky in a private B2B message | "But you are free" evidence; meeting-first asks perform worst (`../linkedin-messages/`, vendor data) | practice (inference) |
| A framework should be used as a checklist and an order, never cited as proof of performance | All of the above | practice, resting on weak measured evidence (one small order test with no persuasion to reorder; the hierarchy review) |
